utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please. And good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, distinguished gentlemen and ladies. Yes, I can follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution. MR. DI FAZIO: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Di Fazio, and I appear with my colleague Mr. Doria this morning. And I might also add, my case manager, Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you all. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the colleagues from the OTP. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones, I represent the Defence for Mr. Oric. We have our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, with us, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good morning, everyone. I take it there are no preliminaries. That's what I have been told. So we can proceed straight away. Witness, Mrs. Milovanovic, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am the Presiding Judge in this trial against Mr. Oric. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from Malta. Not the Malta which is in your area but the island of Malta. I am flanked to my right with Judge Hans Henrik Brydensholt from Denmark, and to my left, by Judge Albin Eser from Germany. You are here because you have been summoned by the Prosecution as a witness in this case. Our Rules require that before you start giving evidence, you make a solemn declaration, something which is equivalent to an oath. The purport of the solemn declaration is -- it says that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is contained in a piece of paper which Madam Usher, who is standing to your right, will soon be handing to you. Could I please ask you to stand up, take the text in your hands, read that text aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. You may sit down. You will be here for a very short time. So relax. You don't have to feel nervous or afraid of anything. We will try to do our best to get you out of this courtroom as quickly as possible. The procedure is a very simple one, and I will try to explain it to you. Mr. Jose Doria, on behalf of the Prosecutor, will be asking you a few questions. I understand you have met him before. And then after he has finished, you will be asked questions by Madam Vidovic, at your left, who is representing, who is lead counsel for Naser Oric. Then as soon as it is over, you can go. Your duty, in terms of the oath, the solemn declaration that you have made, is to answer all questions truthfully, honestly, and fully, to the best of your knowledge, and that means answering all questions irrespective of who is putting them to you. In other words, you do not have a right to distinguish between questions coming from the Defence from questions coming from the Prosecution. Your duty is to answer them truthfully, all of them. Having said that, I just want to know, to make sure of two things, whether I have made myself clear to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in your language as we go along. Because we will not be speaking, you will be the only person speaking your own language, and later on Madam Vidovic. The rest of us speak English, so I want to make sure that everything is being translated to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And also I want to make sure that the level, the sound level, is neither too high nor too low for you, that it is okay, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Mr. Doria, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Witness, is that correct that your name is Vojka Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that you were born on the 22nd April, 1956?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that you are of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that you are a housewife?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that you have two children, Dalibor, born in 1980, and Daliborka, born in 1983?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that you used to live, and are still living, in the village of Sase?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that your husband was named Milisav Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that he was born on 18th February 1950?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that you got married in 1977?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Now, witness, can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, where did he work, your husband? Where did he work before the war started?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He worked at the mine in Sase.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And until when he stayed working there?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Do you know if at the time when the war started your husband was enlisted for military service too?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And he used to stay at your village, or he went somewhere else to -- for military duties?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Do you recall if your husband was -- he ever left your house to live somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, how was your relationship with your husband?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was excellent, as good as it can get.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: By the time when the war started, can you tell the Trial Chamber, what was the ethnic composition in your village?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was mixed population, the Muslims and Serbs living together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And they continued to live together after the war started?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, until April 1992, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: What happened after April 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims moved out to Srebrenica, and the Serbs remained in Sase.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Can you recall when was the first attack -- when was it that the first attack occurred against the village of Sase?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in late May, there was some shooting. I jumped out the window and broke my leg. But this was just an attack of small intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And then, I suppose, you returned back to your village.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I returned to the village. And in late October, I was in hospital; rather, I was in hospital and I returned in late October.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And what happened in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In December we were forced to pull out of Sase. We came under attack in Sase. Bjelovac fell. This was on the 16th. And it was across the hill that we pulled out in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And did you stay, you and your husband, together in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And what happened there, after?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I went to Serbia to see my children. The children were in Serbia. Upon my return, I found my husband, who was assigned to Glogova to provide security for the road. I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Did you try to find out what happened?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to find out. They told me he was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Who told you about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My husband's brother, Svetozar, told me so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Do you know how he came to know about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He set out to take some food to Milisav, and then he found out that Milisav had called upon him, Svetozar, also to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Did he surrender?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P39, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Witness, I will help you to understand what is said there. The translation is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What did you -- what does the witness have, a text -- a document in English? Oh, in B/C/S. So what's the problem? Why cannot she read it? Is it because it's too small?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it. It's too small, the print.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Doria, or your case manager, can we have it on Sanction, and can we blow it up a bit, zoom ... Usher, I think you will need to put it either on computer evidence or -- I don't know with regard to the witness what you have to do but ... Oh, I see, I don't blame her. I didn't know it was handwritten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam, if you can read it, it's okay. If you can't read it, it's okay as well. Don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't read the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. What I suggest, Mr. Doria, is that you start reading in English, and the interpreters will translate into B/C/S, and that way she will know what the contents of the documents are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right? I'm sorry you have to do this. Otherwise, I'll do it myself. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Doria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the date of capture of your husband?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 24th December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that your husband was born in Obadi?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sase, Obadi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is it correct that he had eight years of military school?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Witness, you already told us that he used to work for a mining company in Sase since 1970. Is that correct, that he was a skilled flotation worker?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, too, that your maiden name is Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P48 -- P458, please, page 46.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't make this out either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't worry about it, madam. We'll find the solution to that. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Doria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Witness, is that correct, that your husband was a son of Radoje and Slavojka Daganovic from Kostanovka?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that you yourself are from Bukava Gelva [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is that correct, that your husband had five brothers, one Svetozar, born in 1947 --

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: -- and a second -- the second, Stanislav, born in 1952?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And the third, Miodrag, born in 1954?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And the fourth, Dobrislav, born in 1957?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: And Predrag, born in 1960?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Witness, after you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Doria. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Before we leave this exhibit, could you give an explanation where this document is from, P49, because it cannot be recognised, where it comes from. Who is the author of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I'm asking the Prosecutor, Mr. Doria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Exhibit P458 is -- we think that it was a war diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have some more information on this, when it was tendered into the evidence? MR. DI FAZIO: If I may be of assistance, if Your Honours please. I don't have Racine Manas's log here. I can look that matter up, and perhaps later in the proceedings I can convey the information to Mr. Doria and assist Your Honour with that inquiry. That would be the primary -- the immediate source of information as to where it came from. And I can also see if there's any other evidence that the Prosecution has presented, or may be in a position to present, regarding its origins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But this relates only to 458. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: How about P49? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I can do the same, the same exercise with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Doria, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes, if I may add, please. Exhibit P49 is also a document in our record that we think it was written by someone who conducted an interrogation of Mr. Milisav Milovanovic. But we will find out more and give this information to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Witness, after knowing about the capture of your husband, did you have any -- had you any communications with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Did you try to find thereafter what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I found out that he was in prison in Srebrenica. Dostana Filipovic told me that after her exchange. She told me that Milisav was in prison. Later on, sometime in February, when Ratko Nikolic was released, he told me that Milisav had been killed in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Witness, let's go back a little bit. Concerning Dostana Filipovic, do you know who Dostana came to know about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: She saw Milisav in prison. That's what she told me. She told me she had seen him in Srebrenica, in the prison there, and at that time he was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Did Dostana know your husband before the war?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Did Dostana also know what was the nickname of your husband?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: What was the nickname of your husband?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mico.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Did she tell you more about the conditions in the prison where your husband was?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: She told me that when she had seen Milisav, he had been all black and blue. He had been beaten. The conditions were extremely poor, and he was not even allowed to look up. People said, when Milisav saw Dostana in prison, he was not even strong enough to turn around and face her, because he had been beaten that badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Do you remember when Dostana told you about that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. I think it was in late January, but I can't say for sure. I met Dostana in Bratunac. I heard that she had been exchanged. So I went there to see her, but I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: The second person who told you things about your husband was Ratko. That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Da.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I may, we have an objection concerning this piece of evidence, and I can take it very shortly. It's basically this: We've checked the evidence of the transcripts of Ratko Nikolic, and he wasn't actually asked, wasn't even asked about whether Mico died in the cell. In those circumstances, our objection is that, when Ratko Nikolic was here, on oath, giving evidence, that where he's not asked about that, that it's wrong, in those circumstances, to get the evidence secondhand, because if Ratko Nikolic had been asked, he might have said, "No, I never saw any such thing." That's our objection. I can appreciate that Your Honours may not wish to either take my word for it or review the transcripts of Ratko Nikolic's evidence. So it's really, just to get on the record that that's our objection, and that if subsequently you agree that he wasn't asked about whether Mico died in the cell or not, and that goes obviously to the weight of this evidence, and we submit that it's inadmissible, because it's hearsay. But where -- the part -- the person who had the evidence was here, was not asked, and could have given that evidence. I just want to place that on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken, Mr. Jones. Obviously I look at it more as a submission than an objection. Obviously, I cannot stop the witness from saying what, according to her, Ratko Nikolic told her. And obviously, when we put everything in a basket, if what you have submitted is correct, in other words, that Ratko Nikolic never mentioned anything or because he was never asked about this, that, of course, will be taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we can't really consider it, at least according to me, as an objection as such in the true procedural sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I do put it forward as a point of admissibility. It's for Your Honours to take as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but again ... Yes, Mr. Doria, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: When did you meet Ratko Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I met him, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Around the 26th of February, or thereabouts. When he was released from prison and exchanged, I went straight to the house in which he was staying with family, in Bratunac. He told me that Milisav had been badly beaten. And once he was already dead, they wrapped him up in a blanket and took him to the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall being called by someone else to give information concerning your husband?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you can -- no damage. You can go direct. Just -- you can lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: In your written statement, you say that people from the Red Cross came to see you, asking information about your husband; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, you mean that. Yes. Yes, that's true. They asked questions. I gave a statement, what sort of clothes he had on, that sort of thing, how tall he was, how much he weighed. I gave two statements for the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Did they show you anything, like clothes, shoes, photographs of such things?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They came over to Sase to see me, and they brought photographs, files with photographs, in order for me to try and identify some of the clothing, but I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Did you inquire before them whether -- where those photos were from? Was that a result of an exhumation that they conducted?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there had been an exhumation, and they took photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Was there anyone else who gave you information concerning your husband?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Do you remember a certain Bosniak coming to see your brother, informing him about your husband?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This Bosniak used to work with my husband before the war. He met my brother in Bratunac. He told him that he knew the location of Milisav's grave. I went to the police. And those people came over from, I'm not sure what it's called, the digging people. They looked all over the place, but they couldn't find Milisav in the location that the other man had given.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Do you know why you couldn't find the body of your husband there? Is that because the Bosniak lied to you or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I don't think that's an appropriate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you rephrase your question, Mr. Doria, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Bosniak was lying. He took us to a place that was not the right place. Milisav wasn't there when we came. And then he started, sort of, trying to weasel his way out of it. He said he no longer knew where Milisav was. He said he had seen the pit dug, and he said he didn't know who had dug the pit, but that Milisav had already died and that he had been buried there. But he was sort of starting to bend about the bush.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Is there anyone else that gave you information about your husband, apart from those you mentioned? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My neighbours, Bosniaks, all of them returning, claim that Milisav had been buried in Srebrenica, at the cemetery near the church. They all know that Milisav had been killed in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Based upon the information that you got from people, different people telling you, do you believe that your husband is dead?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: What makes you so sure that he is dead and not hiding, for example, somewhere?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why would he be hiding for 12 years? He has no where to hide for that long. He is dead, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Doria. Madam Vidovic. Again, the usual recommendation to allow a pause between question and answer, because now, madam, you will both be speaking in Serbo-Croat and you need to allow a space of time, an interval of time, between question and answer so that the interpreters can translate to us in English, and to some also in French. Thank you. Madam Vidovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Milovanovic, it's correct, isn't it, that Sase is a small village. Before the war it had about 550 inhabitants, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's true that it's a small village, but I can't be sure about the number of inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that before the war, Sase was predominantly Muslim? About 440 Muslims lived there.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you would agree, wouldn't you, that Muslims were, by far, the predominant group in relation to the Serbs in Sase.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea what the predominant group was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You remember that you spoke to the OTP in July 2004. You do remember that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated at the time that the war in Sase had begun on the 17th and 18th of December, when the Muslims attacked. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. The Muslims attacked earlier as well, on the 12th of July as well, I mean they attacked Sase.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that at the beginning of the war, the Muslims left Sase. You said the Muslims went away.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you said the Muslims started to attack Sase from the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why would the Muslims leave and go to the neighbouring villages to live there as refugees only to be able to attack their own homes in Sase from there? My submission to you is 80 per cent of the houses there were Muslim anyway.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: They weren't attacking their own homes, they were attacking Serb homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The truth is quite different from what you're saying, isn't it, Mrs. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Muslims were being continually attacked in April and May of 1992, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that between the 9th of May, 1992, from that date on, in Sase there was a Territorial Defence unit made up of the local Serb population under the command of Milorad Todorovic, and it was referred to as the Sase Territorial Defence unit?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your husband was a commander of that unit, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's true that he was mobilised, but I have no idea who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This unit literally massacred the Muslim population of Sase on the 22nd of May, 1992, and burned down their homes. This is something that was happening near where you lived. You were in a position to know, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was in hospital at that time. I went to the hospital on the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Mrs. Milovanovic, you did say a while ago that you went to the hospital in late May.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct, late May, about the 20th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. As early as April 1992, while you were still in Sase, and in early May 1992, there was a notorious camp in Sase where Muslims were being detained; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But the camp was in the vicinity of the Sase mine where your husband used to work, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. My husband continued to work until as late as February.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Mrs. Milovanovic, Sase is a very small village, and all Serbs knew about this, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What's more, Mrs. Milovanovic, the local Serbs were, in fact, in charge of the camp and they mistreated the detainees. This is something that people talked about, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Milovanovic, can you tell the Chamber, please, what the distance is between the hamlet of Gradina and your own home?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The distance is not great.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you specify, please?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: About 1 kilometre, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point hear that, on the 20th of May, which is the day that you referred to, that on the 20th of May, alone, in one day, 53 Muslims were arrested in Gradina and sent to the camp?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that only 11 of them survived that day? I'm talking about your neighbours from Sase.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any time hear that, not far from you, 18 small children from Sase were killed, natives of Sase?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Milovanovic, this could not be concealed. I'm sure Serbs talked about this, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not among the women. We were in our homes. We were housewives. This is not the sort of things that we would be told.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Milovanovic, your information on this should be far more comprehensive, I should say. You were, after all, a member of the army of Republika Srpska in 1992, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I returned from hospital, from Serbia, in late October, and I stuck to my kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the 4th Sase Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say yes?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said yes. Late October.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Milovanovic, I'll ask you something else now. Was your husband born in Obadi or in Andrici?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Andrici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood that a while ago the transcript registered that he was born in Obadi.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was registered, being on the books as being born in Obadi, but actually he was born in Andrici.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which hamlet did you live in prior to the 24th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sase.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In a hamlet belonging to Sase, or in Sase itself?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In Sase.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that your husband's brother, Svetozar Milovanovic, told you that your husband had been captured on the 24th of December, 1992, in Glogova; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your husband had gone to Glogova on military business; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your husband was no deserter, was he?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He did not go to Glogova as a form of punishment, did he?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea why he went there, but he was off. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But he was no deserter, was he?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the usher's assistance, please. I would like to know the witness P458, page 03593169. It continues on the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The corresponding English page?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's the same exhibit that the witness has looking at a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the page in English? Because if we're to follow in English, we need to know which page we are supposed to go to.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thirty-one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thirty-one, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Milovanovic, a while ago the Prosecutor showed you information that relates to your husband. On the page with the ERN 03593170, it reads: "Punished as a deserter and forced to go to Glogova." That is not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I merely wish to draw your attention now that we have an objection that we raised with respect to the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. How do you -- at least from the English text, I cannot connect it to Milisav Milovanovic, I connect it to another person. I won't mention the name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this logbook is a little confusing, that's true. But if you look at the original text, it reads: "Milovanovic, Milisav," the date is the 13th of January, and then it continues on page 46. And then on page 47, and it reads exactly as I said: "Arrested in Glogova. Punished as a deserter and forced to go to Glogova." This is clear enough in the Bosnian language. But I've just looked at the English, and I don't think this has been translated. We can have the Bosnian version on the ELMO, please, perhaps that can be of assistance to us, so the interpreters can see for themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... say, madam, I would think, at least trying to put two and two together here, that it could never refer to Milisav Milovanovic, who was married, but to Stanislav Milovanovic. In fact, what we have on page 31, the very first three words is "he is single," and then "arrested in Glogova, as punishment for desertion deported to Glogova." So if he was single, then it couldn't be Milisav Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at any rate, when I look at the B/C/S version, that's what I read. However, can we please have the original provided. And this is the reason why we were adamant on having the original version used right from the outset. I'm just trying to point out some discrepancies in this logbook. This logbook contains a number of facts that are simply not true. I do have further reasons for wanting to use the original text. For the time being, my submission is that this war logbook is simply not an authentic document. At any rate, I was just confronting the witness with a fact. But I can put my question like this, if you like:

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, what about Mr. Stanislav, was he a deserter?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Stanislav Milovanovic, your brother-in-law, was no deserter either, was he?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Milovanovic, your husband was also a member of the Bratunac Brigade, was he not?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This statement that you gave to the OTP that I mentioned a while ago contains the following statement: "The last time I saw him in Bratunac, he was wearing a camouflage uniform, underneath which he was wearing a pair of jeans and a blue and white sweater." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the sort of uniform that was worn by other soldiers from his unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When was your husband given this uniform?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But do you remember whether it was at the beginning of the war or at some later stage, when you had already returned from hospital?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned from hospital, I saw the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So already in October 1992, he had this camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Svetozar Milovanovic did not witness the capture of his brother, did he?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He only heard about it when -- that he had been calling upon him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: He heard that his brother had been calling upon him to surrender?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Milovanovic, is it true -- it is true that you are receiving an allowance, a survivor's benefit, on behalf of your husband from the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could I have the usher's assistance to place D45 on the ELMO, the list of the combatants killed belonging to the army of Republika Srpska, from 1992 to 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: From the Bratunac Brigade, that is. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document please be placed on the ELMO, specifically the page containing the number 369, that is, from item 343 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Milovanovic, please look at the name under item number 369. It reads: "Radoje Milisav Milovanovic, that is, born on the 18th of February, 1960, in Sase," date of his being killed, 24th of December, 1992, in the village of Glogova. And as the date at which this fact was established, it is specified here, the 1st of June, 1993. Your father's -- your husband's father's name was Radoje, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The 18th of February, 1960 is the date of your husband's birth; isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We keep receiving the interpretation of 1960, when it's 1950, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Milovanovic, I will show you another document belonging to the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could I have the usher's assistance. Please place on the ELMO a document by the military post of Bratunac, number 02075870, dated 23 May 1993, entitled "Lists of Villages Torched in the Municipality of Bratunac, Lists of Those Wounded and Killed by Settlements, and Witness Statements."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness please look at the page 02075889, the list of those killed in Glogova, and item 11: Milisav, son of Radoje Milovanovic, 1950, Sase, date of him getting killed 24th of December, 1992." Ms. Milovanovic, do you not agree that these are background data belonging to your husband.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't agree with the date of his death, 24th.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question concerns something else. Do you not agree that these are personal data of your husband's?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document was produced four, five months after the disappearance of your husband, the 23rd of May, 1993, and it says that he got killed on the 24th of December, in Glogova, and not in the Srebrenica prison. Don't you agree this is what the document says?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was captured on the 24th, in 1992, and was killed in Srebrenica on the 24th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you not agree that the documents I showed to you indicate that your husband was killed on the 24th of December, 1992, in Srebrenica? That's what the documents show.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Milovanovic, these are two separate official documents of the army of Republika Srpska, of the Bratunac military post, talking about your husband getting killed on 24 December 1992. The Bratunac military post had no other data on his death prior to this date here.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, because he was filed as missing. And because of my allowance that I was supposed to receive, and I was entitled to receive, I had to report his date of disappearance. And since he disappeared in Glogova, I had to report that particular date, that he had disappeared in Glogova on the 24th. It was later on that we found out that he was killed in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Milovanovic, I put to you that until that date, you had no other information at your disposal. Had you had other information, you would have forwarded it to the brigade that you were a member of, wouldn't you have?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You would have inquired after your husband through the brigade that both you and he were a member of -- were members of.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did inquire after him, but I was unable to find anything out.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be assigned an exhibit number, the list of those killed in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, there's no objection from the Prosecution, but I wonder if we might, at some stage, be given a full copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that will be taken care of by the Defence. I see Madam Vidovic nodding.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour. But I just wish to say that we received this document in the latest disclosure batch, some 10 days ago, from the Prosecutor. But by all means, we shall provide a copy at once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you should have a copy of this. MR. DI FAZIO: I retract my statement. In fact, there was a copy here after all and I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's give it an exhibit number. D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be D172.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: D172. Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Ms. Vidovic, I had the usual question which I asked the Prosecution before. Who has produced this document, D172? Because in the English version, it only speaks of military post number 784, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, according to what we -- the information we received from the Prosecutor as to the source, was drafted by the Bratunac military post. It is a document belonging to the Bratunac military post. And the paper was drafted by Dragan Azivanovic, a clerk working for the Bratunac military post. And here you have the reference number and the date when the document was produced. However, this is just one document out of a large group of documents produced by the Bratunac military post. And this document here that we received through disclosure from the Prosecutor is just one of those. Your Honours, this perhaps should not be discussed in the presence of the witness, but I would like to invoke again Rule 68, because this is something that came under that disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously you can get Ms. Manas to enlighten us on this. Yes, any further questions, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few more. I believe that I will finish very soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Milovanovic, you said that you had received information about your captivity of your husband in Srebrenica from Ratko Nikolic. It is true, is it not, that Ratko Nikolic did not know your husband from before the war?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, he didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is true, is it not, that immediately after his exchange, Ratko Nikolic went to hospital, and you could not talk to him?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I talked to him right away, as soon as he was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Ratko Nikolic did not tell you that he saw your husband die.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dostana Filipovic did not tell you anything about your husband's death in the prison.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Dostana didn't tell me this; she just told me that she saw him in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you have no reliable information as to his death in the prison, except for what you had heard.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. I only know what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did have some information about the possible sites of burial of your late husband in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All these sites were dug up and searched.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not all of them. There are some more sites that will probably be processed this spring.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the sites which you were told could be the places where your late husband's body might be found. That's what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. There's one more location --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name of the location.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I put to you that this particular site was also dug up.

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, there's another one that -- this one was processed, but I'm not referring to this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever the case, Ms. Milovanovic, your late husband's body has not been found in Srebrenica to date. That's the truth, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKA MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination? I take it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, Mr. Doria.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that your husband was born in Obadi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I think that's clear enough. She said that he's registered as having been born in Obadi, but in actual fact he was born in Andrici or --

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: Andrici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Andrici. So for the Tribunal, for the Trial Chamber, that's clear enough. You don't need to waste time on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DORIA
utterances.text: We have no more questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to have been so abrupt, but it's just -- it's clear enough for us. Do you have any questions? Do you have any questions? I don't have any questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'll deal with this later, shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- your testimony ends here. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher out of this courtroom, and after that you will receive all the assistance that you require to make it possible for you to return home as early as possible. On behalf of the Trial Chamber and of the Tribunal, on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and on my own behalf, I should like to thank you for having accepted to come over and give testimony in this case. And before you leave, on behalf, again, of everyone present here, I should like to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I just add something, in the end?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask Mr. Oric to tell me where my husband's bones are. He probably knows where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think that's a very unfair comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. Okay, Mr. Oric has heard you, has heard what you said, madam. Okay, you will be escorted out now of the courtroom. I can't address Mr. Oric in the courtroom or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the first thing we need to tell you is that we have gone through your reply to the Prosecution's response to your motion, and have considered the suggestion or -- let's call it suggestion, by the Prosecution to be considered -- to have considered the possibility of a response to the reply to the response to the motion. Our decision is in the negative. The matter ends there. We have already started studying the import of the motion and the response and the reply, and hopefully next week we should be in a position to hand down a decision. If we need any further help from, assistance from you, obviously we'll give you time for some oral presentations, but that's about it. And I don't think, things being what they are at the moment, unless we come to that decision, that there will be any further discussion on this. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you for that clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Just in reply to Judge Eser's question earlier during the course of this witness' testimony. At the moment what I can tell you is P49 was tendered on the 8th of October -- 8th of October, last year. Apparently the source is Dan Perry from Major Ranko Todorovic, and it's one of the documents from the Sokolac -- what's been referred to in this case as the Sokolac collection. And it was put in evidence through Ms. Manas. P458, apparently I wasn't here in court on the day, but it was produced in evidence through Nikola Popovic on the 9th of December 2004, so the surrounding testimony you'll find on that particular date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any further business to transact? None? We will not be sitting tomorrow, we will be sitting on Monday. We will be sitting in Monday, and I don't remember whether it's in the morning or the afternoon. In the afternoon, yes, because I'm sitting on another case in the morning. Yes. I thank you, and have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To be reconvened on Monday, the 31st day of January, 2005, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.20 a.m.
